lessons.title: Your First C++ Program
lessons.description: Program structure, standard output, the build pipeline, and the path from a source file to execution inside Nexus.
theory: Your first C++ program is not about memorizing “Hello, C++!”. It is a compact way to see several layers at once: source text, the standard library, main, standard output, the build pipeline, and execution.

C++ source code is not executed as plain text. Build tools parse and validate the program according to the language rules and prepare an executable representation. Diagnostics therefore usually belong to a specific stage of that path.

#include <iostream> makes stream I/O declarations available, std::cout names the standard output stream, and operator << inserts data into that stream. These are connected language/library concepts, not magic boilerplate.

Inside Nexus, beginner code runs in the integrated browser sandbox. You do not need to install a desktop IDE or separate compiler for the core exercises: editor, standard input, run controls, and output live in the lesson.
lessons.deep: From the beginning, separate four concepts: the C++ language, the code editor, the compiler/runtime, and the operating system. An IDE may combine several tools in one window, but it is not the language itself. Nexus Sandbox plays the educational role of an integrated environment while remaining accessible through a browser on desktop and mobile devices.
lessons.analogy: Think of a production line: the source file is the specification, preprocessing prepares the materials, the compiler validates and transforms parts, the linker assembles the product, the runtime prepares the work area, and main begins the user-written scenario.
lessons.commonMistake: Memorizing the program shape as a ritual and assuming that Visual Studio, VS Code, or another IDE “runs C++” by itself. The language, editor, build tools, and execution environment are separate layers.
lessons.task: Modify the program to print three lines: your name, “I am learning C++”, and an IT field that interests you. Use std::cout and '\n'.
lessons.hint: Use three sequential output operations. Each line can use its own std::cout statement.

benchmark.whyItMatters: This lesson defines the mental model used throughout the course. Instead of memorizing a Hello World template, we connect source text to the standard library, build tools, process execution, and the integrated Nexus environment. Compiler diagnostics, the sandbox, and later C++ topics then become parts of one system.
outcomes: Read a minimal C++ program and explain every construct instead of reproducing it from memory.
Distinguish the C++ language, source files, an IDE, a compiler, a linker, a runtime, and an operating system.
Explain source file → preprocessor → compiler → object code → linker → process startup → main.
Explain #include <iostream>, std::cout, ::, <<, string literals, \n, and return 0.
Classify common failures as preparation, compilation, linking, or runtime problems.
Run, modify, and validate code directly in Nexus Sandbox without requiring an external desktop IDE.
prerequisites: It is enough to know that a program is a formal sequence of instructions.
No prior experience with Visual Studio, VS Code, terminals, or compiler internals is required.
A basic everyday distinction between text and numbers is helpful; data types are taught later.
All new terminology is expanded in this lesson glossary.
quickUnderstand: C++ is the language. main.cpp is a text source file. An editor only helps you write that text.
#include <iostream> makes standard stream declarations available; it does not “insert a finished program”.
int main() defines the special main function. After startup work, normal user-written execution reaches it.
std::cout is standard output. std:: identifies the namespace and << inserts values into the stream.
"Hello, C++!\n" is a string literal; \n represents a newline.
A semicolon terminates a statement, braces delimit a block, and return 0 reports successful completion.
Nexus Sandbox combines editor, stdin, execution, and stdout in the browser, so beginner exercises do not require an external IDE.

fullTheory.lead: A minimal C++ program is tiny only in source-code size. Behind those lines are the language, standard library, preprocessing, compilation, linking, process startup, and function execution. This section follows the entire path and explains how Nexus reproduces the learning workflow inside the browser.

sections.title: 1. Language, source code, and editor are different layers
paragraphs: C++ is a programming language: rules of syntax and semantics. It is not a specific editor and not one compiler implementation.
Source code is text written according to those rules. A .cpp file is still an ordinary text file.
An editor or IDE helps create and manage that text. Visual Studio, VS Code, CLion, and Nexus are environments; none of them is the C++ language itself.

sections.title: 2. The .cpp extension and translation units
paragraphs: The .cpp extension conventionally marks C++ source files. Larger projects may contain many .cpp files plus .h or .hpp headers.
Each source file is usually processed as its own translation unit after preprocessing. The compiler analyzes that resulting unit.
This architecture allows large projects to be built in parts and later combined by the linker.

sections.title: 3. The preprocessor and #include
paragraphs: #include <iostream> is a preprocessing directive. The # at the beginning marks work that happens before the main C++ compilation phase.
A useful beginner model is that the preprocessor locates the requested header and makes its declarations visible in the translation unit.
Including a header does not run a library and does not execute code at runtime. It prepares information the compiler needs.

sections.title: 4. iostream and the standard library
paragraphs: iostream is a standard C++ header for stream I/O. I/O means Input/Output.
It provides declarations for stream objects and related operations such as std::cin, std::cout, and std::cerr.
The C++ standard library provides reusable types and facilities so programs do not need to reimplement strings, containers, streams, algorithms, and many other building blocks.

sections.title: 5. Namespaces, std, and ::
paragraphs: Large programs can contain identical short names from different components. Namespaces group names and help avoid collisions.
Most of the standard library lives in namespace std. std::cout means “cout from std”.
The double colon :: is the scope-resolution operator. Explicit qualification helps beginners see exactly where a name comes from.

sections.title: 6. main and the beginning of user code
paragraphs: A function is a named unit of executable logic. main has special status: in a normal OS-hosted program, user-written execution begins there after startup work.
int main() declares main as returning an int and taking no parameters in this form.
The operating system does not necessarily jump directly to main as the first machine instruction. Runtime startup code may execute before control reaches it.

sections.title: 7. Blocks, statements, and semicolons
paragraphs: Curly braces delimit a block. Here they define the body of main.
A statement is a complete instruction. Many C++ statements end with a semicolon, which is syntax rather than decoration.
Whitespace often does not change C++ meaning, but formatting strongly affects human readability.

sections.title: 8. std::cout and operator <<
paragraphs: std::cout is the object connected to standard output. In a terminal this usually appears as text; in Nexus it appears in the result panel.
In this context << is the stream insertion operator: std::cout << value sends a representation of value into the stream.
Insertions can be chained, for example std::cout << "x=" << x << "\n";.

sections.title: 9. String literals, escape sequences, and \n
paragraphs: Text inside double quotes is a string literal. The quote characters mark its boundaries.
Escape sequences encode special characters: \n is newline, \t is tab, and \" represents a quote inside a string.
The backslash indicates that the next character participates in a special notation, so \n is not two ordinary printed characters.

sections.title: 10. Buffering, \n, and std::endl
paragraphs: Output is often buffered so many small operations can be combined efficiently.
\n inserts a newline but does not by itself require an immediate flush. std::endl inserts a newline and also flushes the stream.
Both may look identical in a tiny example, but unnecessary flushes can be costly, so Nexus uses \n as the normal default.

sections.title: 11. return 0 and process exit status
paragraphs: return ends a function and sends a value back to its caller. In main, the returned integer becomes the process exit status.
By convention, zero indicates success while non-zero values often signal different failures.
For main specifically, reaching the closing brace without an explicit return is treated as return 0. We keep the explicit line in the first lesson for clarity.

sections.title: 12. Syntax, semantics, and diagnostics
paragraphs: Syntax asks whether code is written according to the grammar. Missing semicolons, quotes, or braces are common syntax problems.
Semantics concerns the meaning of recognized constructs: whether names exist, types match, and operations are valid.
Compiler diagnostics describe where the tool can no longer build a valid model. The real cause may be on the previous line.

sections.title: 13. Compilation, object code, and linking
paragraphs: A compiler translates a source unit into a lower-level representation and traditionally an object file.
The linker combines object files and required library definitions into the final program. A source unit can compile successfully and still fail at link time.
Distinguishing compile and link failures is essential because they require different fixes.

sections.title: 14. Runtime, process, and standard streams
paragraphs: When a program starts, the operating system creates a process with memory and other resources.
Runtime support prepares the environment used by user code. Some initialization may occur before main.
A process usually has stdin, stdout, and stderr. Nexus presents the relevant input and output streams in the lesson interface.

sections.title: 15. IDE, compiler, and Nexus Sandbox
paragraphs: IDE means Integrated Development Environment. It combines editing, navigation, running, debugging, and related tools, often by invoking a separate compiler toolchain.
VS Code is primarily an extensible editor/platform; native C++ usually requires an installed toolchain. That dependency is inconvenient for mobile-first education.
Nexus Sandbox provides an educational C++ runtime directly in the browser. Editor, stdin, run controls, output, and saved lesson state remain inside one learning environment.

sections.title: 16. Cross-platform learning and sandbox boundaries
paragraphs: Standard C++ aims for portability, but compilers, operating systems, and platform libraries can differ. Portable examples avoid unnecessary environment-specific extensions.

The current Nexus browser runtime targets educational C++ examples. It is ideal for syntax, algorithms, and core structures but is not a replacement for every capability of a production native toolchain.
As the platform grows, the same Sandbox UI can select different runtime providers while keeping the learner inside Nexus.

lessons.title: Pointers, References, and Addresses
lessons.description: The address model of memory: object, address, pointer, reference, lifetime, and safe access without mystique.
theory: A variable has a value, but a live object also has a location in the program's address space. An address denotes that location; a pointer can store such an address as its own value.
The expression &value obtains the address of value. If p has type int*, p can store an address of an int. The expression *p dereferences p and accesses the int at the stored address.
The declaration int& ref = value creates a reference—an alias for the existing object. Writing through value, *p, or ref can modify the same object when they are all connected to value.

Address-based code must respect lifetime. A pointer may still contain a numeric address after the target object has died; dereferencing such a dangling pointer is undefined behavior. Modern C++ therefore prefers RAII, containers, and smart pointers for ownership.
lessons.deep: Core model: value is one int object with a value and an address; p is a separate pointer object storing that address; *p accesses value through the address; ref is another name for value. They are related but not identical.
lessons.analogy: A building has an address; a note containing that address is like a pointer; a second name for the same person is like a reference. The note is not the building, and the second name does not create a second person.
lessons.commonMistake: Confusing p, &value, and *p. p is the stored address; &value obtains value's address; *p accesses the object through that address. The symbols * and & also have different meanings in declarations and expressions.
lessons.task: Create n = 3, make ptr point to n, and use *ptr so the program prints 12. Then print n and *ptr separated by a space and verify that they match.
lessons.hint: After int* ptr = &n;, the expression *ptr denotes the same object n through the stored address.

benchmark.whyItMatters: Pointers are not mysterious C++ magic; they are an explicit way to work with the address model. This model underlies arrays, function interfaces, linked structures, polymorphism, resource management, and many libraries. The goal is to keep object, address, pointer, and alias conceptually separate—and then connect them safely.
outcomes: Distinguish an object's value, its address, and a pointer's value.
Read int*, int&, &value, p, *p, and ref by context.
Explain nullptr, dangling pointers, lifetime, and undefined behavior.
Compare pass-by-value, pointer parameters, and reference parameters.
Understand basic const forms for pointers and references.
Use Nexus Sandbox and the interactive memory model to validate predictions.
prerequisites: You only need basic variables, expressions, and functions.
No prior knowledge of stack/heap, new/delete, or machine addresses is required.
Addresses shown by Nexus are symbolic teaching addresses, not browser memory addresses.
quickUnderstand: value is one int object with a value and an address while it is alive.
&value obtains value's address.
int* p declares a pointer to int; p is a separate object.
p = &value stores value's address in p.
*p dereferences the pointer and denotes the target object.
int& ref = value creates an alias for value rather than a second int.
nullptr means the pointer intentionally points to no object; it must not be dereferenced.
An address is usable only while the target object remains alive and the access is valid.

fullTheory.lead: Do not memorize punctuation first. Build one stable model: a live object, its address, a separate pointer storing that address, a reference aliasing the object, and lifetime rules governing valid access.

sections.title: 1. Object, value, and storage
paragraphs: int value = 10; creates an int object whose logical state is 10. During execution the implementation also needs storage for that state.
We model a live object as having an address in the process address space. The numeric address can change between runs and is rarely important by itself.
Keep language semantics separate from a literal memory diagram: C++ exposes address operations, but an optimizer may represent objects differently as long as observable behavior is preserved.

sections.title: 2. Address-of operator &
paragraphs: The expression &value means “obtain the address of value”. Here & is the unary address-of operator.
The result type is related to the target type: the address of an int has type int*.
The address is not a copy of value's number. It is a separate value that can later be used to access the object while lifetime rules remain satisfied.

sections.title: 3. A pointer is its own object
paragraphs: int* p; declares p as an object capable of holding the address of an int.
After int* p = &value;, p stores value's address. p and value remain two different objects.
Pointer size is platform/ABI-dependent and should not be confused with sizeof(int).

sections.title: 4. The two roles of *
paragraphs: In int* p, * participates in the declaration and says p is a pointer to int.
In the expression *p, * is the dereference operator and denotes the object at p's stored address.
Therefore *p = 25; changes value when p points to value.

sections.title: 5. A reference is an alias
paragraphs: int& ref = value; binds ref to the existing object value.
ref = 30; changes value because ref is another name for that object.
Assigning ref = other later does not rebind an ordinary reference; it assigns other's value to the already-bound target.

sections.title: 6. p, &value, *p, and ref
paragraphs: value denotes the object in an ordinary expression; &value obtains its address; p stores an address; *p denotes the target; ref is an alias.
When p == &value and ref is bound to value, writes through value, *p, or ref are observable through the other access paths.
This is aliasing: multiple expressions may denote one object.

sections.title: 7. nullptr and pointer checks
paragraphs: nullptr is the modern C++ null pointer literal: it represents an intentional “points to no object” state.
Storing or comparing nullptr is valid; dereferencing it is not.
A non-null check does not prove that a pointer is otherwise valid or that the target is still alive.

sections.title: 8. Lifetime and dangling pointers
paragraphs: Lifetime is the interval during which an object exists according to the language rules.
If a pointer retains the address of a local object after that object dies, the pointer becomes dangling.
Dereferencing a dangling pointer causes undefined behavior even if the numeric address still looks plausible.

sections.title: 9. Undefined behavior
paragraphs: Undefined behavior (UB) means the C++ standard imposes no required behavior after certain rules are violated.
This is not the same as a normal exception or a guaranteed crash. Optimizers may rely on the assumption that valid programs do not execute UB.
Pointer safety requires reasoning about initialization, lifetime, type, and bounds—not merely syntax.

sections.title: 10. Function parameters: value, pointer, reference
paragraphs: int x receives a copy; changing x does not change the caller's object.
int* p receives a copy of an address and may modify *p after validating the pointer.
int& x is an alias for the caller's object. const int& provides non-copying read access while preventing mutation through that reference.

sections.title: 11. const and access direction
paragraphs: const int* p is a pointer to const int: p may be redirected, but *p may not be modified through p.
int* const p is a const pointer to int: p's stored address is fixed, but the target int may be modified.
const int* const p combines both restrictions; const int& is a common read-only reference form.

sections.title: 12. Pointers and arrays
paragraphs: An array and a pointer are not the same type, but array names convert to pointers to the first element in many expressions.
For a pointer into an array, p + 1 advances to the next element of the pointed-to type rather than one byte.
Pointer arithmetic is only valid within carefully defined bounds of the same array object.

sections.title: 13. Dynamic storage and modern C++
paragraphs: new can create an object with dynamic storage and returns a pointer; delete ends the corresponding lifetime and releases storage.
Manual new/delete is error-prone, so modern C++ usually prefers automatic objects, containers, and RAII.
std::unique_ptr expresses unique ownership; std::shared_ptr is reserved for genuine shared ownership. Raw pointers remain useful for non-owning observation and low-level interfaces.

sections.title: 14. Stack and heap are implementation models
paragraphs: Teaching often says locals live on the stack and new allocates on the heap. That can be a useful implementation model but is not the full language definition.
The standard talks about storage duration, lifetime, and observable behavior; optimizers may keep values in registers or eliminate objects entirely.
Nexus therefore uses symbolic addresses to teach relationships rather than claiming to display the browser's physical memory layout.

sections.title: 15. Why this unlocks later topics
paragraphs: References and pointers let functions work with existing objects without mandatory copies.
Linked structures represent connections between nodes; low-level implementations often use pointers or smart pointers.
Runtime polymorphism is commonly used through base-class references or pointers, making this lesson foundational for OOP.

sections.title: 16. A practical safety checklist
paragraphs: Before dereferencing, ask: is the pointer initialized, non-null, still pointing to a live object, and within valid type/bounds rules?
If you cannot justify those conditions, change the design or add the appropriate invariant/check rather than hoping for a crash you can catch later.
In modern application C++, prefer values, references, containers, and RAII by default; use raw pointers when their semantics are deliberate and clear.

lessons.title: OOP: Encapsulation, Inheritance, and Polymorphism
lessons.description: Designing your own types: state, invariants, interface, inheritance, and dynamic polymorphism without magic.
theory: Object-oriented programming (OOP) organizes parts of a program around types and objects that combine state with permitted operations. In C++, OOP complements algorithms rather than replacing them.

A class describes a type; an object is a concrete instance of that type at runtime. Data members hold state, member functions implement behavior, and the class contract defines which state transitions are valid.

Encapsulation is broader than the private keyword: it means preserving invariants through a controlled interface. Inheritance models specialization, while runtime polymorphism lets a common base interface dispatch to behavior of the actual derived object.

Modern C++ combines OOP with composition, RAII, generic programming, algorithms, and value semantics. Deep inheritance trees are not a goal; use inheritance only when it represents a stable type relationship.
lessons.deep: The central OOP question is not “how do I write class?” but “who owns this state, who may change it, and what guarantee does the type make to the rest of the program?” A class with private fields can still be poorly encapsulated if its interface allows inconsistent states.
lessons.analogy: A bank account stores a balance, but a client does not edit the database number directly. The client performs allowed operations such as deposit, withdraw, and query. The interface protects domain rules.
lessons.commonMistake: Treating encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism as a checklist for every project. Good C++ uses classes when they simplify responsibility; composition often beats inheritance, and a public interface should remain small.
lessons.task: Create a Wallet class with a private balance field. Its constructor accepts the initial balance, deposit(int amount) accepts only positive values, and getBalance() returns the current balance. Create Wallet(1000), deposit 250, and print 1250.
lessons.hint: Keep balance private. In deposit, validate amount > 0 before changing balance. External code should use methods rather than writing the field directly.

quickUnderstand: A class describes a type; an object is a concrete instance.
Object state lives in data members; methods define permitted operations.
private blocks ordinary external access and helps the class preserve invariants.
A public interface is a promise to callers and should usually remain small.

fullTheory.lead: Build one model in order: user-defined type → object state → invariant → public interface → composition → inheritance → virtual dispatch. Then the classic OOP terms become engineering tools instead of slogans.

sections.title: 1. OOP as responsibility design
paragraphs: Procedural thinking asks which steps to perform. Object design adds: which component owns this state and is responsible for keeping it valid? The approaches work together; a method still contains an algorithm.
The benefit appears at scale: local type rules reduce the number of places that can accidentally break state.
C++ is multiparadigm, so OOP is a tool rather than a mandatory religion.

sections.title: 2. Class and object are different
paragraphs: class Counter { ... }; describes a type. It does not create a particular counter object.
Counter c(10); creates a concrete Counter instance with its own value state.
Many objects may share one class definition while each object has its own identity, state, and lifetime.

sections.title: 3. State, behavior, and invariant
paragraphs: State is the current values of an object's data members; behavior is the set of operations offered by the type.
An invariant is a condition that must remain true for a valid object—for example, a balance may be required to stay non-negative.
A good class is built around invariants: construction creates a valid state and public operations do not let callers break it.

sections.title: 4. private, public, and protected
paragraphs: private members are inaccessible to ordinary external code and separate implementation details from the public contract.
public members form the external interface. The less callers know about internals, the easier implementation changes become.
protected exposes members to derived classes and should be used carefully because wide protected state tightly couples an inheritance hierarchy.

sections.title: 5. Encapsulation is broader than private
paragraphs: A class may have private fields and still be poorly encapsulated if it exposes trivial setters/getters that allow contradictory states.
Encapsulation is control: the object enforces its rules through meaningful operations such as deposit(), withdraw(), or rename().
The public API should express domain actions rather than mirror raw storage.

sections.title: 6. Construction and valid initial state
paragraphs: A constructor participates in object creation and should establish a coherent initial state.
Counter(int start) : value(start) {} initializes value before entering the constructor body.
Invalid inputs need an explicit contract: reject construction, normalize only when that behavior is intentional, or report failure appropriately.

sections.title: 7. const member functions
paragraphs: int get() const promises not to modify the object through the ordinary const contract.
This allows the method to be called on const objects and documents observation rather than mutation.
const-correctness is part of the type's interface: it communicates which operations are state-changing.

sections.title: 8. Composition: objects containing objects
paragraphs: Composition models has-a: Car has an Engine; Order has LineItems.
Composition is often simpler than inheritance because dependencies are explicit and reusable components do not claim a subtype relationship.
Start by considering values and composition; use inheritance when callers genuinely need a common type.

sections.title: 9. Inheritance and is-a
paragraphs: class BonusAccount : public Account defines a derived type. Public inheritance usually promises that BonusAccount can be used where Account is expected.
The derived class receives the accessible base interface and may add specialization; private base state does not become directly accessible derived state.
Inheritance only for code reuse creates brittle designs. Reuse and subtyping are different goals.

sections.title: 10. virtual and dynamic type
paragraphs: A non-virtual call is selected from static type information. A virtual call through a base interface may select an override based on the actual dynamic type.
If Account& view refers to BonusAccount and kind() is virtual, view.kind() can execute BonusAccount::kind().
The C++ standard specifies behavior but does not require a particular vtable layout. A virtual table is a common ABI technique, not a literal language object.

sections.title: 11. override as intent checking
paragraphs: override marks a derived member that is expected to override a virtual base member.
If the signature is accidentally different, the compiler reports the problem instead of silently creating an unrelated overload/member.
It is a low-cost automatic check of architectural intent.

sections.title: 12. Base references and pointers
paragraphs: Runtime polymorphism is commonly used through Base& or Base*. A reference fits a required object; a pointer can represent optionality/address semantics.
A base reference does not copy the derived object, so the dynamic type remains derived.
This is why pointers and references were a prerequisite for the OOP benchmark.

sections.title: 13. Object slicing
paragraphs: Copying a derived object by value into a base object discards the derived part because the destination is a separate Base object.
Polymorphic APIs therefore commonly take Base& or Base* rather than Base by value.
Slicing demonstrates how value semantics and object models interact in C++.

sections.title: 14. Abstract classes and pure virtual functions
paragraphs: virtual void draw() = 0; is pure virtual. A class with a pure virtual function is abstract and cannot be directly instantiated.
Such a type can express a common interface that concrete derived classes must implement.
Use abstract interfaces when the system genuinely needs interchangeable implementations under one contract.

sections.title: 15. Virtual destructors in polymorphic bases
paragraphs: If a derived object may be destroyed through a pointer to the base, the base destructor must be virtual as part of that design.
Otherwise deleting through Base* can cause undefined behavior and incomplete destruction of the derived object.
This applies to polymorphic bases intended for that ownership/deletion pattern.

sections.title: 16. Practical modern C++ design
paragraphs: Start with simple values, small types, and explicit invariants. Add inheritance/virtual only when a real common interface and substitutability are needed.
Prefer composition for implementation reuse and RAII for resource management.
A strong class reduces the number of invalid states callers must reason about and makes incorrect operations difficult or impossible.

lessons.deep: A handler can generate another action: adding a task may require refreshing a list. Immediately invoking another handler increases stack depth and can expose partially updated state. lessons.deep: An event source and its receiver can disappear at different times. Checking expired and then dereferencing a raw address does not establish the same ownership contract.

lessons.title: Responsive work, bounded steps and cancellation
lessons.description: Split work into bounded steps and cancel without committing a partial result.
theory: Split work into bounded steps and cancel without committing a partial result.
lessons.deep: In a single-threaded application, a handler occupying the event loop prevents the next user command from running. A fast average case does not guarantee responsiveness on larger input. Divide the operation into portions and return control to a scheduler between them. Bound both the number of calls and the work performed inside each call.
lessons.analogy: size specifies total work, done counts processed items and candidate stores a provisional result. Reason about step to establish 0≤done≤size. The local budget decreases on every iteration and done grows only up to size. Each call therefore handles at most three items even when the complete job requires many calls.

lessons.title: Model persistence and format versioning
lessons.description: Implement a checkable roundtrip and candidate-based loading that preserves the old model on failure.
theory: Implement a checkable roundtrip and candidate-based loading that preserves the old model on failure.
lessons.deep: Saved data may outlive a program version. A format needs an explicit marker and field definitions. Teaching format EV1 stores an element count and values in 0…100. A future EV2 cannot be guessed to mean EV1: identical numbers might have different meanings. Reject unknown versions before mutation, and treat migration as a separate checkable algorithm.
lessons.analogy: load first validates version and count, then constructs a separate candidate vector. It validates every value before appending it and checks end of input after the last item. Only a completely valid record permits model.swap(candidate). Before swap the model still holds its previous data, so rejection requires no manual restoration of overwritten elements.
lessons.task: The format is EV1 count values, with count=0…8, values=0…100 and whitespace-only trailing input. Failure preserves old model {99} and prints rejected 99. On success save in memory, reload into a copy and compare; stdout is the canonical EV1 record.

lessons.title: Event testing and reproducible traces
lessons.description: Check a model through traces, invariants, replay and a controlled implementation mutation.
theory: Check a model through traces, invariants, replay and a controlled implementation mutation.
lessons.deep: An event-driven defect may require several actions. One add call says little about add→complete→complete or import→failure→save. A test needs initial state, an ordered trace, observations after steps and an expected outcome. Removing unnecessary events from a failing trace helps find a minimal reproduction.
lessons.analogy: replay takes a const vector and creates fresh local state. It reads no clock, random seed, window or global counter. Two invocations on the same trace must return equal Results. A C++20 defaulted == compares value and rejected; adding another field should trigger a review of the observable contract.

theory: Connect TaskModel to real Qt widgets and execute a user scenario inside Nexus.
lessons.deep: Qt is an additional library, not part of standard C++. It requires its own SDK and build toolchain. In Nexus select Project Studio, create a C++ application and open src/gui.cpp. Building compiles your C++ to Qt/WebAssembly and opens a separate Preview. The lesson’s console Clang/WASI editor contains no Qt and cannot run this exercise.
lessons.analogy: QApplication initializes the graphical environment. TaskWindow derives from QWidget and QVBoxLayout arranges controls vertically without manual coordinates. QLineEdit accepts text, QPushButton represents an action, QListWidget displays tasks and QLabel presents status. Passing this as a parent makes child QObjects owned by the window, so they are not separately deleted when the parent is destroyed.
